Flattereth
flăt'ter-eth
v. (third person singular of flatter: to praise falsely for advantage; to make smooth with the tongue; rendering Hebrew chalaq)
Old French flater, to stroke or smooth with the hand. The Hebrew chalaq means to be smooth, to divide, to apportion — a smooth tongue and a divided heart are the same word.

Biblical Definition

Flattery in Scripture is a weapon, and Proverbs treats it as one. It begins at home: “he flattereth himself in his own eyes, until his iniquity be found to be hateful” (Psa 36:2). Self-flattery is the first and most successful lie a man tells, and it works precisely by keeping the sin from ever looking hateful to him. Then the strange woman, twice: Wisdom is given to deliver thee from “the stranger which flattereth with her words” (Pro 2:16; Pro 7:5). Then the talebearer: “meddle not with him that flattereth with his lips” (Pro 20:19) — the man who is warm to your face collects secrets to spend elsewhere. Then the great reversal: “He that rebuketh a man afterwards shall find more favour than he that flattereth with the tongue” (Pro 28:23). The rebuke wins in the end; the flattery only wins now. And the plainest of all: “A man that flattereth his neighbour spreadeth a net for his feet” (Pro 29:5). Flattery is not excessive kindness. It is trapping, and Solomon calls it a net. Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to flatter as to please by artful commendation or compliments; to gratify self-love by praise or obsequiousness; to encourage by favorable notice.

expand to see more

FLATTER, v.t. To please by artful commendation or compliments; to gratify self-love; to sooth by praise.

2. To please; to gratify; as, to flatter one's vanity or pride.

3. To raise false hopes in, by praise or representation; to encourage by favorable notice.

Key Scripture

Psa 36:2 — "For he flattereth himself in his own eyes, until his iniquity be found to be hateful."

Pro 28:23 — "He that rebuketh a man afterwards shall find more favour than he that flattereth with the tongue."

Pro 29:5 — "A man that flattereth his neighbour spreadeth a net for his feet."

Modern Corruption

Flattery has become the ordinary register of encouragement, and a generation taught to affirm everything has lost the faithful wound of a friend.

expand to see more

Proverbs 29:5 is one of the most counter-cultural verses in the book because it classifies flattery not as excessive niceness but as trapping: a man that flattereth his neighbour spreadeth a net for his feet. The net is the point. Flattery works by telling a man what he wants to hear until he walks confidently into ground he would have avoided had anyone told him the truth. A whole vocabulary of affirmation now stands ready for this purpose, and it is genuinely difficult to tell encouragement from flattery by the words alone, because they are frequently the same words. Scripture gives the test in the next verse-pair rather than in the vocabulary: he that rebuketh a man afterwards shall find more favour. Encouragement is willing to say the hard thing and takes the short-term cost; flattery is not and does not. The pastoral loss is severe. A church in which no one has ever been told a difficult truth about himself has no friends in it in the biblical sense, only well-wishers — and Psalm 36:2 warns that the man nobody will correct will finish the job himself, flattering himself in his own eyes until his iniquity is past finding hateful.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chalaq (H2505), to be smooth, to divide, to flatter; cheleq, smoothness of speech; Greek kolakeia (G2850), flattering words, used of Paul's refusal in 1 Thessalonians 2:5.

expand to see more

Hebrew chalaq (H2505) — to be smooth, and so to divide or apportion; the smooth tongue and the divided heart share one root; Psalm 36:2, Proverbs 2:16, 28:23.

Hebrew chelqah — smoothness, a smooth place; Jacob's neck was smooth, and so is the strange woman's mouth; Proverbs 5:3, Genesis 27:16.

Greek kolakeia (G2850) — flattery, flattering speech used as a cloak of covetousness; Paul denies ever using it; 1 Thessalonians 2:5.

Usage

"“He flattereth himself in his own eyes” — the first and most successful lie."

"“More favour than he that flattereth with the tongue” — the rebuke wins in the end."

"“Spreadeth a net for his feet” — flattery classified as trapping."
